svg.title: Scalar vs SIMD lanes with fma()
svg.desc: Two arrays of eight doubles, q and v1, sit in rows of cells on the left. A scalar loop walks them one index per step: each step multiplies one pair and adds the product to a single accumulator cell that starts at zero, so the dot product takes eight steps. On the right, a 256-bit DoubleVector has four lanes of 64-bit doubles. Each step loads four doubles of q into register a and four of v1 into register b, and fma() multiplies and adds all four lanes into a four-lane accumulator, also zero at first, so two steps cover the eight elements. Then reduceLanes adds the four lanes into one double, 1.44, and the vector loop is done while the scalar loop is still on step four. Both loops end with the same 1.44: eight steps against two steps and one reduction.
svg.text: Scalar vs SIMD lanes with fma()
A scalar loop does one multiply-add per step. DoubleVector.fma() does one in each lane: 4 per step at 256 bits.
scalar loop: one multiply-add per step
Vector API loop: four lanes per step
Two loops compute the same dot product, q · v1 over 8 doubles: a scalar loop on the left, a Vector API loop on the right.
Per step, the scalar loop does one multiply-add. fma() does four, one in each lane of a 256-bit DoubleVector.
Two steps cover all 8 doubles. Then reduceLanes(ADD) adds the 4 lanes into one: 0.14 + 0.24 + 0.57 + 0.49 = 1.44.
The vector loop is done. The scalar loop is only on step 4 of 8, adding one product at a time.
Same result, 1.44. The scalar loop took 8 steps; the vector loop took 2 fma() steps and one reduceLanes().
Sources: openjdk.org/jeps/537 (JEP 537: Vector API) and netflixtechblog.com (Optimizing recommendation systems with JDK's Vector API).
